name: Shattered-Chapel
specific_features: Debris ring from ancient moon collision
Surface fractures arranged in radial patterns from a central impact
description: Shattered-Chapel is a small, airless world that bears the unmistakable scars of a catastrophic collision that nearly tore it apart. A central impact crater spans nearly a third of the planet's diameter, and from it radiate fracture lines that extend across entire hemispheres like the cracked glass of a broken window. The impact expelled enough material to form a thin debris ring that catches starlight in a faint, glittering halo around the equator.

Without atmosphere, the surface exists in stark binary: blinding illumination on the sunlit side, absolute darkness on the far. Temperature swings are extreme and rapid, the rock expanding and contracting with each rotation in a cycle that slowly grinds the surface to regolith. The silence is total and absolute, broken only by the vibrations transmitted through boot soles when rock shifts beneath a walker's weight.

Geological analysis suggests the collision occurred approximately two billion years ago, when a moon-sized body struck at an oblique angle. The planet survived intact only because the impactor was largely composed of ice, which vaporized on contact rather than transferring its full kinetic energy into the crust. The exposed mantle intrusions at the crater's center reveal mineral compositions found nowhere else in the system, materials forged in the heat of that ancient apocalyptic moment.

Shattered-Chapel's platinum group deposits, concentrated along the fracture lines by the impact event, represent one of the richest accessible veins in the sector. Mining operations are straightforward in the low gravity and vacuum, requiring only basic pressure suits and standard extraction equipment. The primary hazard is the debris ring, which occasionally sheds fragments that strike the surface without warning, a reminder that the collision that made this world profitable is still, in geological terms, ongoing.
